title: The Late Pleistocene Megafauna Extinction
intro: Between roughly 50,000 and 10,000 years ago, most land mammal species weighing over 44 kg went extinct across Australia, Eurasia, and the Americas. Two scientists discuss the cause.

figures.label: Scientist 1
figures.caption: Overkill hypothesis
figures.text: The extinctions were caused primarily by human hunting. The timing of the losses tracks the arrival of modern humans on each landmass rather than any global climate event: Australia lost its megafauna around 45,000 years ago, shortly after human arrival, while North America lost its megafauna about 13,000 years ago, again shortly after human arrival. Africa, where hominins and megafauna coevolved over millions of years, retained most of its large mammals — precisely what one would expect if naive prey animals were the vulnerable ones. Large, slow-reproducing species need only a small sustained increase in mortality to decline toward extinction; models show that a kill rate of a few animals per hunter per year is sufficient over centuries.

figures.label: Scientist 2
figures.caption: Climate hypothesis
figures.text: The extinctions were caused primarily by rapid climate change at the end of the last glacial period. Between 15,000 and 11,000 years ago, warming fragmented the cold, dry, productive "mammoth steppe" into forest and wetland, collapsing the habitat that supported grazing megafauna. Pollen records show vegetation turnover preceding or coinciding with the losses on multiple continents. Direct kill sites are rare: fewer than 20 North American sites show unambiguous evidence of humans butchering mammoths or mastodons, far too few to account for continent-wide extinction. Moreover, several species survived for millennia alongside humans before disappearing, which is inconsistent with rapid hunting-driven collapse.

title: What Caused the Younger Dryas Cooling?
intro: About 12,900 years ago, the Northern Hemisphere abruptly cooled by several degrees for roughly 1,200 years, reversing a warming trend. Two scientists discuss the cause.

figures.label: Scientist 1
figures.caption: Meltwater hypothesis
figures.text: A vast glacial lake in North America drained suddenly into the North Atlantic. The influx of fresh water reduced surface salinity and density, weakening the ocean circulation that carries warm water northward. Weakening that circulation cools northern Europe and eastern North America while leaving the Southern Hemisphere little changed — exactly the asymmetric pattern the ice-core and pollen records show. Sediment cores from the St. Lawrence outlet record a discharge event at approximately the right time.

figures.label: Scientist 2
figures.caption: Impact hypothesis
figures.text: A comet or asteroid fragmented over the ice sheet, triggering continent-scale wildfires whose soot blocked sunlight and initiated cooling. A thin sediment layer dated to 12,900 years ago contains elevated platinum, magnetic microspherules, and nanodiamonds at dozens of sites across three continents — materials associated with extraterrestrial impacts and not produced by lake drainage. The abruptness of the onset, within decades, favors a sudden catastrophic trigger over a gradual oceanographic change.

title: Three Explanations for Desert Varnish
text:
Desert varnish is a thin, dark coating of iron and manganese oxides that forms on exposed rock surfaces in arid regions. It can take centuries to accumulate a layer less than a millimeter thick, and the coating darkens further the longer it remains exposed. Three geologists studying the same varnished rock outcrop proposed different explanations for where the coating's minerals originally come from.

Geologist 1
Geologist 1 argues that the varnish forms from within the rock itself. Many desert rocks contain small amounts of iron and manganese bound up in their internal mineral structure. Geologist 1 proposes that rainwater rarely but occasionally seeps into surface cracks and pores, where it slowly dissolves these trace minerals. The water then evaporates quickly, which is typical of an arid climate. As it evaporates, it deposits the dissolved iron and manganese as a thin film on the rock's outer surface. Repeated over thousands of cycles of wetting and evaporation, this film thickens into visible varnish. Under this view, the varnish's composition should closely mirror the mineral makeup of the rock beneath it. The coating, in this account, is made from material that migrated outward from the rock's own interior rather than arriving from anywhere else.

Geologist 2
Geologist 2 rejects a purely chemical explanation and points instead to microorganisms living directly on the rock surface. Certain bacteria are known to gain usable energy by chemically oxidizing manganese, a process that leaves behind solid manganese oxide as a byproduct. Geologist 2 proposes that these bacteria colonize the rock surface in a thin biological film. As they grow, the bacteria absorb trace manganese and iron carried by windblown dust and moisture, and deposit the oxidized metals directly onto the rock. Because the responsible organisms are living things rather than a passive chemical process, this hypothesis makes a distinct prediction. A rock's varnish should be able to form even on rock types that contain little or no iron or manganese of their own, since the metals arrive from outside sources rather than leaching from within the rock.

Geologist 3
Geologist 3 attributes the varnish almost entirely to windblown dust. Deserts generate large quantities of fine airborne particles, some of which carry trace iron and manganese picked up from distant soils. Geologist 3 proposes that this dust settles continuously on exposed rock surfaces. Thin films of moisture from dew or occasional rain bind the particles to the rock and to each other, gradually cementing them into a hardened crust. Because the source of the minerals is external dust rather than the rock's own composition or living organisms, this hypothesis makes a distinct prediction of its own. Varnish from different rock outcrops in the same region should share a similar chemical makeup regardless of what kind of rock lies underneath, since all of the outcrops in an area receive dust from the same regional source.

title: Why Is the Blue-Spotted Tree Frog Declining in Cedar Hollow?
text:
Over the past 15 years, the population of blue-spotted tree frogs in Cedar Hollow, a forested wetland, has declined by more than 70 percent. Researchers agree on the extent of the decline but disagree about its primary cause. Three biologists studying the wetland have proposed different explanations.

Biologist 1
Biologist 1 attributes the decline primarily to a fungal skin infection that has been detected on frogs throughout the region. The fungus disrupts a frog's ability to regulate water and electrolytes through its skin, which can be fatal within weeks of infection. Biologist 1 notes that the fungus thrives in cool, wet conditions similar to those in Cedar Hollow, and that infected frogs have been found at every site sampled in the wetland. Under this view, the decline should track the spread of the fungus itself rather than any change in the physical habitat. Populations in wetlands where the fungus has not yet arrived should remain stable, even if those wetlands closely resemble Cedar Hollow in every other respect.

Biologist 2
Biologist 2 points instead to agricultural runoff. Farms upstream of Cedar Hollow began using a new pesticide roughly 18 years ago. Biologist 2 argues that trace amounts carried into the wetland by rainwater have interfered with the frogs' hormone systems, reducing successful reproduction even among adults that otherwise appear healthy. Biologist 2 notes that the timing of the decline follows the introduction of the pesticide more closely than it follows any known arrival of disease. Under this view, reproductive success should be lowest closest to the streams that drain the farmland. Wetlands with no agricultural runoff nearby should show a much smaller decline, even if the fungus described by Biologist 1 is also present there.

Biologist 3
Biologist 3 argues that the decline is best explained by an invasive fish species, introduced to Cedar Hollow's ponds around 20 years ago for recreational fishing, that preys heavily on frog eggs and tadpoles. Biologist 3 notes that ponds within the wetland that remain fish-free still support relatively dense frog populations, while ponds stocked with the invasive fish show far fewer frogs at every life stage. Under this view, the decline should correlate closely with the presence of the invasive fish from pond to pond within Cedar Hollow itself, regardless of disease exposure or nearby farmland. Removing the fish from a pond should allow the frog population there to recover over time.

title: The Trout of Lake Idris
intro:
Lake Idris supported a lake trout population for as long as records exist. Lake trout need cold water and also need dissolved oxygen; in summer the lake separates into a warm surface layer and a cold deep layer, and the fish are confined to whatever water satisfies both requirements. Between 1995 and 2020 the catch fell by more than 90%, and by 2020 no trout were found. Two limnologists proposed different explanations.

Scientist 1

The lake warmed. Mean August surface temperature rose 2.6 °C over the period, and the boundary between the warm and cold layers sank steadily deeper. Each summer the band of water cold enough for trout grew thinner, until in the hottest years it closed entirely for several weeks. Trout that cannot escape warm water stop feeding, grow slowly, and fail to spawn. The decline tracks air temperature almost year for year, and the three steepest single-year drops in catch all followed the three hottest summers on record. Oxygen in the deep layer did fall, but that fall is itself a consequence of warming: a warmer, longer-stratified summer keeps the deep layer sealed off from the air for more weeks each year.

Scientist 2

The lake lost its oxygen. Farm acreage in the watershed doubled after 1990, and the phosphorus entering the lake rose with it. Phosphorus feeds algae; when the algae die they sink and decay, and decay consumes oxygen in exactly the deep, cold water the trout depend on. Measured August oxygen in the deep layer fell from 8.1 mg/L to 1.9 mg/L, well below the 4 mg/L that lake trout require. The cold water never disappeared — it simply became unbreathable. Warming may have made matters worse at the margins, but a 2.6 °C rise in surface temperature does not by itself remove a deep layer that is still 6 °C in August.

title: The Origin of the Ring Structure at Saarat
text:
A roughly circular structure 4 km across sits in flat sedimentary rock in a remote basin. Its rim stands 60 m above the surrounding plain. Three geologists account for it differently.

Geologist 1

The structure is an impact crater. Quartz grains from the rim show planar deformation features, a set of parallel microscopic fractures that form only under shock pressures above 5 gigapascals. No volcanic or tectonic process on Earth generates pressures in that range. The circular shape, the raised rim, and the shocked quartz together admit only one explanation.

Geologist 2

The structure is a collapsed salt dome. A thick salt layer underlies the basin, and salt rises through denser overlying rock, doming it upward. When groundwater later dissolves the salt, the dome collapses and leaves a circular depression with an upturned rim. The planar features in the quartz can also be produced by rapid tectonic movement along a fault, and faults are mapped through this basin. No meteorite fragments have been recovered from the site.

Geologist 3

The structure is a volcanic maar, formed when rising magma met groundwater and flashed it to steam. The explosion excavated a circular crater and threw a rim of debris around it. Basaltic dikes are exposed 9 km to the north, showing that magma reached shallow depths in this basin. Such an explosion generates pressures sufficient to deform quartz, and it leaves no meteorite fragments because no meteorite was involved.

title: Sound Absorption in Wall Panels
text:
When sound strikes a wall, part of its energy is reflected back into the room and part is absorbed. The absorption coefficient (alpha) of a surface is the fraction of the incident energy that is absorbed, so alpha runs from 0 for a perfect reflector to 1 for a surface that returns nothing. A room lined with absorbent panels has a shorter reverberation time than the same room lined with plaster.

Panels were tested in a reverberation chamber. Every panel had a face area of 1.0 m squared. A panel described as mounted flush was fixed directly against the chamber wall; a panel described as mounted on an air gap was held 50 mm clear of it on battens, with the gap left open.

Table 1 gives alpha for a 25 mm panel of open-cell foam, mounted flush, at six frequencies.

Table 2 gives alpha at 500 Hz for four thicknesses of that same open-cell foam, each thickness measured twice: once mounted flush and once on a 50 mm air gap.

Table 3 gives alpha at 1000 Hz for four panel materials, every one of them 50 mm thick and mounted flush, together with the density of each material. The material listed first in Table 3 is the same open-cell foam used for Table 1 and Table 2.

Rooms are usually hardest to treat at low frequencies. A sound at 125 Hz has a wavelength of about 2.7 m in air, while a sound at 4000 Hz has a wavelength of about 85 mm, and a panel only a few tens of millimetres thick sits very differently against those two lengths. Designers therefore quote a panel by the frequency band it is meant to control rather than by a single figure, and a panel chosen for speech may do little for traffic noise coming through the same wall.

title: Spheres Falling Through Oil
text:
A sphere released in a still liquid speeds up until the drag on it balances its weight, after which it falls at a steady terminal velocity. Students measured terminal velocity by timing steel spheres over a 0.50 m section of a tall tube, marked far enough below the surface that the sphere had already stopped accelerating. Every sphere was made of the same steel, of density 7.8 g/cm cubed. The viscosity of a liquid is a measure of its resistance to flow and is reported here in pascal-seconds.

Each trial was repeated three times and the three timings averaged; no timing differed from its average by more than two per cent. Between trials the tube was left to stand until any bubbles raised by the previous sphere had cleared, since a bubble crossing the marked section makes the sphere appear to hesitate. Spheres were recovered from the base of the tube with a magnet, wiped, and reused.

Experiment 1. Four steel spheres of different radii were released in oil A, held at 20 degrees Celsius, at which temperature oil A has a viscosity of 0.20 pascal-seconds. Table 1 gives the terminal velocity of each sphere.

Experiment 2. A single steel sphere of radius 2.0 mm was released in each of four oils, all held at 20 degrees Celsius. Table 2 gives the viscosity of each oil and the terminal velocity of the sphere in it.

Experiment 3. The same 2.0 mm sphere was released in oil A at each of four temperatures. Warming an oil lowers its viscosity. Table 3 gives the viscosity of oil A at each temperature and the terminal velocity measured there.

title: The Mounds at Kerrin
text:
The Kerrin plain carries tens of thousands of low earth mounds, each roughly 2 m high and 20 m across, spread over 40 km of grassland. Seen from the air they stand in a strikingly even pattern, with about 30 m of bare ground between neighbouring mounds. Grass grows taller and greener on the mounds than between them. Three students account for the pattern.

Student 1. The mounds are built. A soil-moving insect colony occupies each one, carrying grains up from below and heaping them at the surface over centuries. The even spacing is the signature of neighbouring colonies meeting at their boundaries and pushing no further, exactly as territorial colonies do elsewhere. Soil brought up from depth should differ from the surface soil around it, and because the colonies are still at work the mounds should still be growing.

Student 2. Nothing builds the mounds. On a dry plain, water soaks in faster where plants already grow, so a patch of vegetation takes more of each rainfall than the bare ground beside it and dries that ground further. The patches that survive draw water from a fixed radius, and that radius sets the spacing. Wind-blown dust settles among the stems and accumulates, and the mound is simply what has piled up. Where rainfall is lower each patch must draw on a wider area, so the spacing between mounds should be wider.

Student 3. The mounds are relics of farming. Several centuries ago the plain was cultivated in planting mounds laid out on a regular grid, and what remains is the eroded remnant of that grid. No living builder is needed and none should be found. The mound soil should carry traces of occupation, such as charcoal or fragments of fired pottery, the field should end abruptly at the old boundaries rather than fading out, and the mounds should be slowly wearing down rather than growing.

Two further observations are available to all three students. Soil taken from the mounds holds more clay than the topsoil between them. Along a rainfall gradient that runs across the plain, mounds in the wetter zone, which receives about 400 mm of rain a year, stand about 30 m apart, while mounds in the drier zone, which receives about 250 mm, stand about 55 m apart.

title: Output of a Photovoltaic Panel
text:
A photovoltaic panel turns part of the sunlight falling on it into electrical power. Irradiance is the power arriving per unit of face area, in watts per square metre. The efficiency of a panel is the power it delivers divided by the power arriving on its face, so a panel of face area 1.6 m squared sitting under an irradiance of 800 W/m squared is being offered 1280 W however much of it the panel manages to use.

One panel of face area 1.6 m squared was tested outdoors on a frame that could be tilted. Tilt angle is measured from horizontal, so a tilt of 0 degrees lies flat and a tilt of 90 degrees stands upright. Cell temperature was measured with a sensor bonded to the back of the panel; it is not the air temperature, and a panel in still air runs well above the air around it.

Table 1 gives the output of the panel at six tilt angles, every reading taken at an irradiance of 800 W/m squared and a cell temperature of 25 degrees C, with the face freshly cleaned.

Table 2 gives the output at five cell temperatures, every reading taken at a tilt of 30 degrees, an irradiance of 800 W/m squared, and with the face freshly cleaned.

Table 3 gives the output for four states of the panel face, from freshly cleaned to a settled film of wind-blown sand, together with the number of days since the face was last washed. Every reading in Table 3 was taken at a tilt of 30 degrees, an irradiance of 800 W/m squared, and a cell temperature of 45 degrees C.

The cells themselves do not choose how warm they run. Sunlight that is not converted is absorbed as heat, so the conditions that offer a panel the most light are the conditions that warm it most, and an installer choosing a mounting has to weigh the light a tilt gains against the air it lets past the back.

title: Testing Antibiotics on Two Bacterial Strains
text:
A bacterium spread evenly over a nutrient plate grows into a continuous lawn. If a small paper disc soaked in an antibiotic is laid on that lawn, the antibiotic seeps outward through the jelly and the bacteria closest to the disc fail to grow, leaving a clear circle called the zone of inhibition. The diameter of that circle is measured in millimetres, and a diameter of 0 mm means the lawn grew right up to the edge of the paper.

A laboratory used the same plates, the same growing jelly, the same 6 mm paper discs and the same 18 hours at 35 degrees C for every test below. Diameters include the width of the disc itself; a disc with no clear zone around it is recorded as 0 mm. The laboratory treated a strain as susceptible to an antibiotic when the zone reached 15 mm or more.

Experiment 1. Four antibiotics, W, X, Y and Z, were each loaded onto a disc at 10 micrograms and laid on separate plates of Strain A. Table 1 gives the zone diameter for each.

Experiment 2. Antibiotic Y alone was loaded onto discs at five different masses and laid on plates of Strain A. Table 2 gives the zone diameter at each mass. The 10 microgram disc in Table 2 is the same test as the Antibiotic Y row of Table 1.

Experiment 3. Experiment 1 was repeated exactly, with the same four antibiotics at the same 10 micrograms, on Strain C instead of Strain A. Strain C had been recovered from a patient who had already been treated with Antibiotic W. Table 3 gives the zone diameters.

A zone says only that growth stopped somewhere. How far the antibiotic travelled through the jelly before it thinned below a useful concentration depends on the size and solubility of the molecule as much as on what it does once it arrives, so two antibiotics with equal zones are not necessarily equally useful in a patient.

title: Why Did the Petrel Colony at Ard Skerry Fail?
text:
Storm petrels are small seabirds that nest in burrows dug into turf and in the gaps under boulders. A pair lays one egg a year, and the chick leaves the burrow about sixty days after hatching. The colony on the island of Ard Skerry has been counted since 1978.

The count of breeding pairs was 4,200 in 1978, 1,900 in 1995 and 190 in 2012. Fledging success, the number of chicks that left the burrow per breeding pair, was 0.71 in 1978, 0.66 in 1990, 0.21 in 1998 and 0.18 in 2010. Brown rats were first recorded on the island in 1991, after a fishing boat grounded on its north shore. Landings of sand eels, the small fish the adults carry back to the burrow, fell by roughly two thirds in the surrounding sea between 1985 and 2000. A severe October storm in 2004 drove seawater across the low southern terrace and flooded the burrows there.

Scientist 1. Rats caused the collapse. Rats take eggs and small chicks, and a burrow offers a chick no defence against one. Fledging success was still 0.66 in 1990 and had fallen to 0.21 by 1998, which brackets the arrival of rats in 1991 and nothing else. Burrows on the high northern slope, which the 2004 storm never reached, failed in the same years and at the same rate as burrows on the southern terrace, so flooding cannot be the general cause. Adults returning to a burrow they have lost a chick in tend to move elsewhere the following year, which is why the count kept falling long after the first rats arrived.

Scientist 2. Food caused the collapse. The count had already dropped from 4,200 to below 3,000 by 1990, before any rat set foot on the island, and the sand eel decline was well under way by then. A chick fed too little does not starve outright; it fledges late and light, and a light fledgling rarely returns to breed. That is why the count keeps falling even in years when many chicks leave the burrow. Rats were present on the neighbouring island of Fara throughout this period, and the Fara colony held steady while its birds fished a different bank.

Scientist 3. Storms caused the collapse. Severe autumn storms became roughly twice as frequent over this period. Flooding kills a chick outright, and it also collapses the burrow, so a pair that loses one must dig again in ground that is now waterlogged. The 2004 storm alone took the whole southern terrace, and the terrace held most of the colony when the counts began. High-slope burrows are dug into thin turf over rock and have always been the poorer ground; that they now fail at the same rate as the terrace says the terrace has been ruined, not that the slope was ever safe.

title: Flow in the River Anwen
text:
A gauging station on the River Anwen, 62 km from the source and draining a catchment of 480 km squared, records stage, which is the height of the water surface above a fixed datum, in metres. Stage is easy to read continuously; discharge, the volume of water passing the station each second in cubic metres per second, is not. Discharge was therefore measured directly with a current meter on 14 occasions spread over three years, and a rating curve was fitted relating stage to discharge, so that every later stage reading could be converted.

Table 1 gives discharge at six stages, read from that rating curve.

Table 2 gives the mean discharge for each month of one calendar year at the same station.

Suspended sediment is the material carried along within the water rather than rolled along the bed. It was measured from bottle samples drawn at mid-depth and expressed as a concentration in milligrams per litre. Table 3 gives concentration at five discharges. The load of sediment passing the station, in kilograms per second, is the concentration multiplied by the discharge, once the units are made to agree: 1 m cubed of water is 1000 L, and 1 000 000 mg is 1 kg.

The rating curve is fitted only over the range of stages at which a direct measurement was made, and the highest of the 14 measurements was taken at a stage of 2.40 m. Readings above that stage can be recorded by the gauge, but no measured discharge exists to anchor them.

The catchment is grazed pasture on clay, with no reservoir and no abstraction upstream of the station. Rain falling on clay reaches the channel quickly, which is why the monthly means in Table 2 follow the rainfall of the season closely rather than lagging behind it by months as they would on a chalk catchment.

All readings were taken at the same station, and no tributary enters between the source and the station.

title: The Pits at Tolven Down
text:
Tolven Down is a chalk ridge carrying a field of 60 shallow pits, each 2 to 3 m across and 0.6 to 1.1 m deep. Fourteen have been excavated. Struck flint flakes were found in 5 of the 14; charcoal lay at the base of 3. A low mound sits immediately beside the hollow in 9 of the 14. The long axes of the pits cluster near 040 degrees; joint sets mapped in the chalk elsewhere on the down run at 038 degrees and 128 degrees. Flint nodules occur in a band about 0.8 m below the surface. Pollen from a nearby bog shows woodland cover on the down until about 3400 years ago.

Scientist 1. The pits are flint quarries. People dug down to the nodule band, which the depths reach almost exactly, took what they wanted, and left. The struck flakes are the waste of working the flint at the pit edge, and the charcoal is from fires at the same working. That only some pits contain flakes is expected, because a quarry is emptied and backfilled, and most debris was carried off to be used elsewhere.

Scientist 2. The pits are solution hollows. Rainwater made mildly acidic by carbon dioxide dissolves chalk, and it does so fastest where joints in the rock let water down. The alignment of the pits at 040 degrees matches a joint set at 038 degrees, which no human plan would reproduce. Nothing about the depths is meaningful: solution stops where the chalk is less jointed, which happens to be near the nodule band because the nodules interrupt the joints. There are no spoil heaps, and a quarry that moved a cubic metre of chalk must leave the chalk somewhere.

Scientist 3. The pits are tree-throw hollows. When a large tree is blown over, its root plate tears out of the ground and leaves a hollow with the root plate, and the soil in it, as a mound alongside. That is exactly the paired shape recorded in 9 of the 14 pits, and it is the only proposal that explains a mound at all. The pollen record puts woodland on the down until 3400 years ago, so the trees were there. Flakes and charcoal are ordinary material of an inhabited landscape and fall into any hollow that is open.

title: Stopping a Test Vehicle
text:
A stop has two parts. Reaction distance is the ground covered between the moment a driver sees a hazard and the moment the brakes begin to act; during it the vehicle does not slow at all. Braking distance is the ground covered from that moment until the vehicle is at rest. Total stopping distance is the sum of the two.

One car, fitted with anti-lock brakes and the same set of tyres throughout, was tested on a closed track. Braking distance was measured from the point of brake application to the point of rest. Reaction distance was not measured but calculated, using a fixed reaction time of 1.0 s, as the distance the car travels at its set speed in that second.

Table 1 gives braking distance at five speeds on dry asphalt.

Table 2 gives braking distance at 60 km/h on four surfaces, every run made at that one speed.

Table 3 gives the reaction distance at the same five speeds, for a reaction time of 1.0 s.

Anti-lock brakes matter to the comparison in Table 2. Without them a hard stop on a slippery surface locks the wheels, and a locked wheel slides rather than grips, which lengthens the stop further and removes the driver’s ability to steer. The system releases and reapplies the brakes many times a second to keep each wheel just short of locking, so every figure in Table 2 is close to the best that surface can give.

The test says nothing about a loaded car, a worn tyre, a slope, or a driver who is tired or distracted. A reaction time of 1.0 s is a convention rather than a measurement, and published estimates of ordinary drivers run from about 0.7 s to well over 2 s depending on how expected the hazard is.

The track was level throughout, the car carried only its driver, and every run began with the brakes cold. A speed of 60 km/h is about 16.7 m/s.

title: A Vibrating String
text:
A steel wire was stretched horizontally over two fixed bridges and tensioned by hanging a known weight over a pulley at one end. The vibrating length is the distance between the bridges. Linear density is the mass of the wire per metre, given here in grams per metre. When the wire is plucked it sounds a lowest, or fundamental, frequency, which was read in hertz from an electronic meter. In every experiment the wire was plucked at its midpoint and the room was held at 20 degrees C.

Experiment 1. Tension was fixed at 40 N and a wire of linear density 0.80 g/m was used. The vibrating length was set to five values in turn. Table 1 gives the fundamental frequency at each.

Experiment 2. The vibrating length was fixed at 0.50 m and the same 0.80 g/m wire was used. The hanging weight was changed to give five tensions. Table 2 gives the fundamental frequency at each.

Experiment 3. The vibrating length was fixed at 0.50 m and the tension at 40 N. Four wires of the same steel but different thicknesses, and therefore different linear densities, were used in turn. Table 3 gives the fundamental frequency of each.

A wire fixed at both ends can vibrate only in patterns that fit a whole number of half-waves between the bridges. The fundamental is the pattern with a single half-wave, which is why it is the lowest note the wire will sound. Higher patterns, sounding at whole-number multiples of the fundamental, are present in every pluck and give the note its character, but the meter was set to report only the lowest.

The condition of a 0.50 m length of the 0.80 g/m wire under 40 N appears in both Experiment 2 and Experiment 3.

title: Why Does Kelm-7 Dim?
intro: The star Kelm-7 dims slightly every 4.0 days. Each dip lasts about five hours and removes about 1.0% of the star’s light before the star returns to normal. Figure 1 shows one dip, measured through a green filter. Table 1 gives the depth of the dip measured through four filters, each passing a different colour of light, averaged over 40 dips. Three astronomers offer explanations.

figures.label: Scientist 1
figures.caption: A transiting planet
figures.text: A planet orbits Kelm-7 once every 4.0 days, and its orbit is lined up so that it passes in front of the star as seen from Earth. A dark planet blocks the same fraction of the star’s light whatever the colour, so the dip should be equally deep through every filter. Once the planet is wholly in front of the star, the fraction blocked stays fixed until it begins to leave, which is why the bottom of each dip is flat. The fraction of light blocked equals the square of the planet’s radius divided by the star’s radius. The dips have arrived on schedule, to within a few minutes, for as long as the star has been watched.

figures.label: Scientist 2
figures.caption: A rotating starspot
figures.text: Measurements of the star’s spectrum show it spins once about every 4 days. A large, cool, dark spot on its surface would turn into view once per rotation and dim the star. Because a spot is cooler than the surrounding surface rather than wholly dark, it removes proportionally more blue light than red, so the dip should be deeper through a blue filter than through a red one. Spots grow and fade over months, so the depth of the dips should drift slowly over a year or more.

figures.label: Scientist 3
figures.caption: An orbiting dust clump
figures.text: Kelm-7 gives off more infrared light than a star of its type should, which is the signature of warm dust around it. A dense clump of dust orbiting every 4.0 days would dim the star as it passed in front. Fine dust scatters blue light more strongly than red, so the dip should be deeper in blue light, and a clump trailing a tail of dust should make each dip fade in quickly but recover slowly.

intro: Tarra is a small island 30 km off the coast. Its lizards belong to the same species as those on the nearby mainland but grow much larger. Table 1 compares the two places. Three biologists explain the difference in size.

figures.label: Scientist 1
figures.caption: Release from predators
figures.text: On the mainland, hawks and shrikes kill most lizards before their third year, so few ever reach full size. On Tarra, with almost no predatory birds, lizards live for many years and keep growing throughout life. Large lizards are also easier for birds to spot, so on the mainland large size carries a cost that it does not carry on Tarra.

figures.caption: Crowding and competition
figures.text: The absence of predators matters on Tarra mainly because it has let lizard numbers climb to nearly eight times the mainland density. Over many generations, crowding has favoured the largest individuals.

figures.text: Tarra is cooler than the mainland. A large body has less surface for each gram of mass, so after basking it loses its warmth more slowly and stays active longer on cool days. On a cooler island, larger lizards can hunt for more hours, and this, not predators or crowding, has driven the increase in size.

title: Why Does Bread Go Stale?
intro: Bread firms as it ages. Firmness can be measured as the force, in newtons (N), needed to squash a slice of crumb to three-quarters of its height. Loaves from one batch were stored for 3 days under different conditions and then tested. Table 1 gives the results, along with the loss of water from each loaf as a percentage of its starting mass. head: Storage

figures.label: Scientist 1
figures.caption: Drying out
figures.text: Bread stales because it dries. Water moves out of the soft crumb, first into the crust and then into the air, and a drier crumb is firmer. An open loaf stales fastest because nothing stops the water escaping. A sealed bag slows the loss, but water still moves from crumb to crust inside the bag, so even a wrapped loaf firms.

figures.label: Scientist 2
figures.caption: Starch crystallizing
figures.text: Baking swells the starch in flour and breaks up its orderly structure. As the bread cools and ages, the long starch molecules slowly line up again into firm crystals, trapping water inside them. This happens fastest at refrigerator temperatures, almost stops in a freezer, and can be undone by reheating, which melts the crystals. Water loss adds to firmness in an open loaf but is not the main cause of staling.

title: Where Did the Moon Come From?
intro: Rock samples brought back from the Moon, and measurements made from orbit, allow scientists to compare the Moon with Earth. Table 1 summarises some of these measurements, along with the same measurements for Mars, which formed in a different part of the solar system. Three scientists explain where the Moon came from.

figures.caption: Earth, the Moon and Mars compared
head: Property
Earth
Moon
Mars
rows: Radius of iron core (fraction of body’s radius)
Oxygen isotope signature (difference from Earth, parts per million)

figures.label: Scientist 1
figures.caption: A giant impact
figures.text: Early in Earth’s history, a body about the size of Mars struck Earth a glancing blow. The impact threw vaporized and molten rock from the outer, rocky layers of both bodies into orbit, where it gathered to form the Moon. Because the Moon was built mostly from rocky outer material rather than from iron-rich cores, it has only a small iron core. The heat of the impact drove off much of the material’s volatile elements, those that boil away easily, such as potassium. The impactor’s material was thoroughly mixed with Earth’s, so the Moon and Earth should share the same oxygen isotope signature.

figures.label: Scientist 2
figures.caption: Formed side by side
figures.text: Earth and the Moon formed at the same time, side by side, from the same ring of rock and dust circling the young Sun. Because they grew from the same material, they share the same oxygen isotope signature. Earth, being larger, drew most of the ring’s iron toward itself, leaving the Moon with little. No violent event was involved, so the Moon should hold about as large a share of volatile elements as Earth does.

figures.label: Scientist 3
figures.caption: Captured
figures.text: The Moon formed elsewhere in the solar system, in a region poorer in iron, and was later captured by Earth’s gravity when it passed close by. This explains why the Moon is so much less dense than Earth. Bodies that formed in different regions of the solar system carry different oxygen isotope signatures, as Mars does, so the Moon’s signature should differ measurably from Earth’s.

title: What Is Heat?
intro: In the early 1800s, scientists disagreed about the nature of heat. Two students each defend one of the historical views, using the results of two experiments. In Experiment 1, samples of water at different temperatures were mixed in an insulated cup and the final temperature was recorded (Table 1). In Experiment 2, a falling weight turned a paddle wheel inside an insulated container holding 500 g of water, and the rise in the water’s temperature was recorded for different amounts of work done by the weight (Table 2). In a separate test, water was weighed before and after being heated from 20 °C to 80 °C; its mass did not change, to within 0.01 g.

figures.label: Student 1
figures.caption: Heat is a fluid
figures.text: Heat is a weightless, invisible fluid called caloric, which flows from hotter bodies to colder ones. Caloric cannot be created or destroyed, so when warm and cool water are mixed, the caloric lost by the warm water is exactly the amount the cool water gains. Rubbing or stirring warms a material because it squeezes caloric out of the material, the way wringing a sponge squeezes out water.

figures.label: Student 2
figures.caption: Heat is motion
figures.text: Heat is the energy of the constant, random motion of the particles that make up matter. When warm and cool water are mixed, the faster particles share their energy with the slower ones until all of them move, on average, alike. Work done on a material, by stirring or rubbing, speeds up its particles, and there is no limit to how much heat can be produced this way for as long as the work continues.

title: Why Do Zebras Have Stripes?
intro: Zebras are the only wild horses with bold black-and-white stripes. Researchers in Kenya dressed tame horses in cloth coats and counted how many horseflies, which bite and spread disease, approached and landed on each coat in 30 minutes (Table 1). They also measured surface and skin temperatures at midday on zebras and on plain-coated horses standing in the same field (Table 2). Three scientists explain why zebras have stripes.

figures.label: Scientist 1

figures.text: Stripes protect zebras from biting flies. Horseflies find their targets by the pattern of light reflected from them, and narrow stripes confuse them as they come in to land, so they fly past or bump off without biting. Flies spread several diseases that kill zebras, so avoiding bites is a large advantage.

figures.label: Scientist 2
figures.caption: Stripes cool the body
figures.text: Stripes keep zebras cool in the hot sun. Black stripes absorb more sunlight and grow hotter than white ones, and the difference sets up small currents of air over the skin that carry heat away. A striped animal should therefore have cooler skin than a plain-coated animal of the same size standing in the same sun.

figures.label: Scientist 3
figures.caption: Stripes confuse predators
figures.text: Stripes protect zebras from lions and hyenas. When a herd of striped animals runs, the moving stripes make it hard for a predator to pick out a single animal and judge its speed and direction, so fewer chases end in a kill.
